---
order: 4
unit: stages
title: Purpose shapes the text
summary: "A text's purpose decides its stages and its language. The same facts about frogs become a report (a general statement, then descriptions, in the present tense with technical words), an argument (a position, reasons and the position restated, with should and would) or a recount (an orientation and events in time order, in the past tense with time words)."
language: maths
node: [AC9E7LA03 n1, AC9E7LA03 n2]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Same topic, two purposes: the recount retells one ride in time order, in the past tense; the report describes what bikes are like, in the present tense." }
hook: "You know ten facts about frogs. Would you put them in the same order to teach Year 3, to win a debate, or to tell your family about an excursion?"
---
A text's **purpose** decides its **stages** and its **language**.

- **Retell what happened: a recount.** Orientation, events, ending. Past tense and time words.
- **Describe what something is like: a report.** General statement, then descriptions. Present tense and technical words.
- **Explain how or why: an explanation.** Opening statement, then steps in order. When, then, as a result.
- **Persuade: an argument.** Position, reasons, position restated. Should, would, because.

## Predict: which shape?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Choosing a shape for a purpose before seeing the models shows students they already link purpose and structure."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Your class found frogs at the creek. You want the principal to let you build a frog pond. Which shape will your text take?"
  options: ["What you want, your reasons, then what you want again", "What happened at the creek, in time order", "Facts about frogs: what they are, then what they're like", "Any shape works if the facts are right"]
  actual: "What you want, your reasons, then what you want again. That is an argument: a position, reasons and the position restated. The facts about frogs become your reasons."
```

## Try: the stages of a report

```step
stage: run
insight: "Labelling a report's stages shows its purpose (to describe) in its shape: say what it is, then describe it."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 340 }
hint: ["Click a sentence, then choose General statement or Description.", "Ask of each sentence: is it about frogs as a whole, or about one part of their lives?"]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "'Frogs are amphibians: animals that live part of their lives in water and part on land.' What is this sentence doing?", options: ["Saying what frogs are", "Describing one detail about frogs", "Giving an opinion about frogs"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "It covers all frogs, not one detail such as their skin.", "There's no should or best here."], explain: "It classifies frogs, so it is the general statement that opens the report." }
check: { type: board, text: "Label the general statement and each description.", when: "n_right = 4 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "The first sentence says what frogs are. Each description covers one aspect: their skin, how they grow, where they live." }
```

Were you right about the pond? The report you just labelled describes frogs; it doesn't ask for anything. An argument would need a different shape.

## Worked example: purpose to stages to language

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Matching purposes to stages, sorting language by purpose and catching Nib's drift show purpose deciding both structure and words."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each purpose to the stages that fit it."
      pairs:
        - ["To retell what happened", "Orientation, events, ending"]
        - ["To describe what something is like", "General statement, descriptions"]
        - ["To explain how or why", "Opening statement, steps in order"]
        - ["To persuade", "Position, reasons, position restated"]
      explain: "Each purpose needs different stages. A writer chooses the stages by asking what the text is for."
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Which kind of text does each sentence's language belong to?"
      options: ["Recount", "Report", "Argument"]
      items:
        - ["On Friday, we visited the museum.", "Recount", "Past tense and a time phrase: retelling."]
        - ["After that, we ate lunch in the park.", "Recount", "After that moves the events along in time."]
        - ["Wombats dig burrows with their front claws.", "Report", "Present tense, about all wombats: describing."]
        - ["Eucalypts are evergreen trees.", "Report", "A general fact with technical words."]
        - ["Our school should build a frog pond.", "Argument", "Should gives a position."]
        - ["A pond would let every class study frogs.", "Argument", "Would imagines a result as a reason."]
      explain: "Recounts use the past tense and time words, reports the present tense and technical words, and arguments words such as should and would."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is Nib's report on frogs, one sentence per line. Click the line where Nib drifts away from the report's purpose."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: purpose-drift
      explain: "Line 3 retells the excursion: past tense, our class, a funny moment. That belongs in a recount. A report describes frogs in general, so Nib should cut it or move it to a recount of the trip."
```

### Purpose decides the stages

```worked
\text{Ask what it is for} :: Retell, describe, explain or persuade?
\text{Choose the stages} :: Each purpose has its own stages (see the list above).
\text{Choose the language} :: Past tense and time words, present tense and technical words, or should and because.
\text{Check for drift} :: Every sentence should serve the one purpose.
```

Now match each purpose to its stages.

## Vary: the same facts, as an argument

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Labelling an argument built from the same frog facts shows how a new purpose regroups the facts into reasons."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 340 }
tasks:
  - starter: "text.yml#vary"
    hint: ["Click a sentence, then choose Position, Reason or Restated position.", "Ask of each sentence: does it say what the writer wants, give a reason why, or press the point again at the end?"]
    check: { type: board, text: "Label the position, the reasons and the restated position.", when: "n_right = 4 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "The position says what the writer wants. The frog facts (clean water to breed, studying them up close) have become reasons. The last sentence restates the position so the reader leaves with it." }
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why does an argument restate its position at the end, when a report doesn't need to?"
      options: ["To leave the reader with what the writer wants", "Because every text must end by repeating its first sentence", "To add a new reason the reader hasn't heard yet", "Because the writer has run out of facts to give"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A report ends when the description is complete. It doesn't need to repeat anything.", "A new reason at the end would need its own paragraph and evidence.", "Restating is a choice that serves the purpose."]
      explain: "An argument's purpose is to persuade, so it ends by pressing the position again. A report's purpose is to describe, so it ends when the description is done."
```

## Practise: language that fits the purpose

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Colouring time words in the recount and technical words in the report shows the language changes with the purpose, even on the same topic."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 340 }
hint: ["Chain 1: words or phrases that move the recount along in time. Chain 2: technical words in the report.", "There are four time words or phrases in the recount, and four technical words in the report."]
check: { type: board, text: "Colour the time words in the recount (Chain 1) and the technical words in the report (Chain 2).", when: "chains_ok = 2 and n_stray = 0", explain: "Last Tuesday, First, Then and After lunch move the recount along in time. Amphibians, tadpoles, gills and metamorphosis name things exactly, which a report needs." }
```

## Make: your own report

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing a report with a general statement and descriptions, in the present tense, applies the purpose-to-structure link."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#make", height: 380 }
hint: ["Pick an animal or a place you know well. Start with what it is: '___ are ___.'", "Add at least two descriptions, each about one aspect, in the present tense. Then label every sentence."]
check: { type: board, text: "Write a report with a general statement and at least two descriptions, and label each one.", when: "has_general = 1 and has_describe >= 2 and n_empty = 0", explain: "Your report says what your topic is, then describes it. Check with a partner: is it all present tense, with no story or opinion slipping in?" }
```

The board checks that the stages are there and labelled. You and a partner check the language: present tense, facts, no drift.

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Naming the purpose before planning a real piece of writing makes the stages a choice, not a habit."
check: { type: reflect, text: "Before my next piece of writing, I wrote its purpose in one line (retell, describe, explain or persuade) and listed the stages it needs before I started." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that a text's purpose decides its stages and its
  language. Using the same frog facts, they label a report's stages, match
  purposes to stages, sort language by purpose, catch a report that drifts into
  a recount, label an argument built from the same facts, colour time words and
  technical words, and write their own report.
time: 50
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 10 min · Practise 7
  min · Make and own writing 13 min
goals:
  - I can say how a text's purpose decides its stages.
  - I can spot language that fits a recount, a report or an argument.
  - I can notice when a text drifts away from its purpose.
  - I can write a report with a general statement and descriptions.
struggle: "Students keep the topic in charge instead of the purpose: they add a
  funny excursion moment to a report because it is about frogs. Nib's drift is
  planted for this. Ask: what is this text for, and does this sentence help?"
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself, then the Vary argument: notice the same facts doing
  a different job.


  The one idea: purpose drives structure, and language follows. This lesson
  covers AC9E7LA03 node 1 (purpose drives structure, a hinge) and node 2
  (language features vary with purpose). The list in the lesson text summarises
  four common types; it is a starting point, not a rule, and the Mixing text
  types lesson shows writers combining them.


  In genre teaching the argument's stages are often called **thesis**,
  **arguments** and **reinforcement of thesis**; the lesson says position,
  reasons and restated position. A report's opening is the **general statement**
  or classification.


  Frog facts (amphibians, skin breathing, tadpoles with gills, burrowing desert
  frogs) and the echidna and eucalypt facts were checked against general
  reference sources.
running:
  - "Predict: ask students to name the stages they'd use before they see the
    list."
  - "Try: ask what a reader learns from the general statement alone."
  - "Worked example: Nib's line 3 is fun. Agree that it is, then ask where it
    would belong."
  - "Vary: put the report and the argument side by side. Which facts became
    reasons? Which were left out, and why?"
  - "Make: partners check each other's reports for past-tense sentences: a sign
    of drift into recount."
stuck:
  - see: A student labels a description as the general statement because it comes
      early.
    ask: Does it say what frogs are, or one thing about them?
    fix: The general statement classifies the whole topic. Descriptions each cover
      one aspect.
  - see: A student colours we or our class as a time word.
    ask: Does this word tell the reader when something happened?
    fix: "Time words place events in time: first, then, after lunch."
  - see: A student's report reads like a recount ('We saw a wombat...').
    ask: Is this about one day you had, or about the animal in general?
    fix: "Use the present tense and talk about all of them: 'Wombats dig...'"
stretch: Rewrite your report as an argument. Which facts become reasons? What do
  you need to add?
support: The purpose list on a card, with one example sentence for each kind of text.
leads: >
  Next in How texts are built: patterns for organising ideas inside a text
  (cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, claim and
  support).


  The argument shape returns in the challenge, Build an argument.
exit:
  q: A text about bushfires is in the present tense, starts 'Bushfires are fires
    that burn through bush and grassland', and uses technical words such as
    ember. What is its purpose and type?
  a: "To describe: it is a report. The general statement and the present tense and
    technical words fit that purpose."
explain: >
  A text's **purpose** decides its **stages** and its **language**.


  - Retell: a **recount** (orientation, events, ending; past tense, time words).

  - Describe: a **report** (general statement, descriptions; present tense,
  technical words).

  - Persuade: an **argument** (position, reasons, position restated; should,
  would, because).


  The same facts can go in any of them. The purpose decides how they are
  arranged.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If you know the facts, does it matter what shape the text takes?
    prompts:
      - Would the principal read a frog report and decide to build a pond?
      - What does an argument do with facts that a report doesn't?
    notes: Facts don't arrange themselves. A report leaves the reader informed; an
      argument leaves them with a decision to make. Same facts, different jobs.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: One fact, three jobs
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Write one fact on the board ("Frogs need clean water to breed"). Pairs
        rewrite it for a recount, a report and an argument.
      notes: Listen for tense changes and should or would appearing in the argument.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Drift check
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Partners swap reports and underline any sentence that slips into another
        purpose (a story moment, an opinion).
      notes: "Ask the writer to decide: cut it, or move it to a different text?"
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which stages?
      type: question
      q: You want to tell your grandparents about the school play you were in. Which
        stages do you need?
      options:
        - Orientation, events, ending
        - Position, reasons, restated position
        - General statement, descriptions
      answer: 0
      explain: You are retelling something that happened, so it is a recount.
```

# Texts for "Purpose shapes the text" (cohesion board). The same frog facts as a report, an argument and a recount.

# region: run
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
roles: general describe
role general: General statement
role describe: Description
s general: Frogs are amphibians: animals that live part of their lives in water and part on land.
s describe: Their skin is thin and moist, and they can take in oxygen through it as well as through their lungs.
s describe: Most frogs hatch from eggs as tadpoles, which have tails and gills, then slowly grow legs and lose their tails.
s describe: In Australia, frogs live everywhere from rainforests to deserts, where some burrow underground during dry spells.
# endregion

# region: vary
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
roles: position reason restate
role restate: Restated position
s position: Our school should build a frog pond in the garden.
s reason: Frogs need clean, still water to breed, and the creek behind the school is getting dirtier.
s reason: A pond would also let every class study frogs up close, from tadpoles to adults.
s restate: For the frogs and for our learning, a pond is worth building this year.
# endregion

# region: practise
widget: cohesion
mode: chain
colours: 2
p: [[Last Tuesday#a]], our class walked to the creek. [[First#a]], we counted the tadpoles. [[Then#a]] we heard a frog calling from the reeds. [[After lunch#a]], we drew what we had seen.
p: Frogs are [[amphibians#b]]. Young frogs, called [[tadpoles#b]], breathe with [[gills#b]]. They change into adults through a process called [[metamorphosis#b]].
# endregion

# region: make
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
roles: general describe
role general: General statement
role describe: Description
tools: text add
s any:
s any:
s any:
# endregion

# region: make-solution
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
roles: general describe
role general: General statement
role describe: Description
s general: Echidnas are small mammals covered in sharp spines.
s describe: They use their long snouts and sticky tongues to eat ants and termites.
s describe: Echidnas are one of the few mammals that lay eggs.
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: cohesion
mode: parts
layout: blocks
roles: recount report
answer: on
s recount: On Saturday, I rode my new bike to the skate park. First I tried the small ramp, and then I raced my sister home.
para:
s report: A bike is a two-wheeled vehicle powered by pedals. Many bikes have gears that let the rider pedal comfortably up hills and on flat ground.
# endregion

# region: nib

Many frogs have long back legs for jumping.
